pioneer10.name: Pioneer 10
pioneer10.eyebrow: NASA · Ames Research Center · Outer-planet exploration · 1972–2003
pioneer10.intro: Before Voyager, a small spinning spacecraft crossed the asteroid belt and entered Jupiter’s radiation environment. Pioneer 10 turned an unknown route into a path other missions could follow, then continued far beyond the planets.
pioneer10.heroAlt: Pioneer 10 spacecraft with its large dish antenna and instrument booms

status.title: Last signal received · 23 January 2003
status.body: Routine science operations ended in 1997. The last telemetry arrived in April 2002, followed by a final faint radio signal in January 2003. There is no current spacecraft contact or live telemetry on this page.

stats.label: High-gain antenna
stats.note: A dish aimed toward Earth for radio communication

exploration.title: Four steps beyond familiar space
exploration.intro: Choose a waypoint to follow the mission from Earth through the asteroid belt to Jupiter and the outer Solar System.
exploration.description: Schematic Pioneer 10 route linking Earth, the asteroid belt, Jupiter and an outward escape trajectory
exploration.note: Illustrative route: distances, angles, planet positions and timing are not to scale. This is a chapter map, not an ephemeris or a current spacecraft position.

stops.name: Leaving Earth
stops.body: An Atlas-Centaur launch began a roughly 21-month journey to Jupiter. The large antenna and spin-stabilised design supported a mission far beyond the orbit of Mars.
stops.factLabel: The first Pioneer sent to an outer planet
stops.question: The launch is often dated 2 March in US histories; it was already 3 March in UTC.

stops.name: The asteroid belt
stops.body: Pioneer 10 became the first spacecraft to cross the main asteroid belt. Dust and meteoroid experiments helped assess a region no spacecraft had traversed before.
stops.question: The belt is not a wall of rocks. Its objects are widely separated, while small-particle impacts still matter to spacecraft design.

stops.name: Jupiter up close
stops.body: The December 1973 flyby measured Jupiter’s magnetic field, charged particles and radiation, while returning close views of its clouds and several moons.
stops.factLabel: Closest height above Jupiter’s cloud tops
stops.question: A flyby is a brief passage. Pioneer 10 did not enter orbit around Jupiter or land on the planet.

stops.name: Beyond the planets
stops.body: Jupiter’s gravity put the spacecraft on an outward escape trajectory. It crossed Neptune’s orbital distance in 1983 and continued returning information from the outer heliosphere.
stops.question: Crossing a planet’s orbit is different from visiting the planet, and different again from crossing the heliopause.

timeline.title: The journey begins
timeline.body: Pioneer 10 launches from Cape Canaveral. It is still the evening of 2 March at the launch site.

timeline.title: The first Jupiter flyby
timeline.body: The spacecraft survives Jupiter’s intense radiation environment and returns a new close view of the giant planet.

timeline.title: Beyond Neptune’s orbital distance
timeline.body: Pioneer 10 passes the outermost planet’s orbit, continuing on an escape trajectory rather than making another planetary encounter.

timeline.title: A final faint signal
timeline.body: Earth receives the last detected carrier signal. The last useful telemetry had arrived on 27 April 2002.

pioneer10.scienceIntro: The mission tested a route, measured a giant planet’s environment and left a radio record that scientists could revisit decades later.

science.title: Testing the asteroid-belt crossing
science.body: Particle and dust measurements helped replace uncertainty about the belt with flight experience, supporting later exploration of the outer planets.

science.title: Inside Jupiter’s magnetic environment
science.body: The encounter measured fields and energetic particles in situ. These data helped engineers understand the radiation conditions later Jupiter missions would face.

science.title: The Pioneer anomaly
science.body: Radio tracking revealed a small unexplained acceleration. A later analysis of Pioneer data showed that uneven heat emission could account for it through photon recoil.

pioneer10.instrumentIntro: Four groups highlight the payload’s different jobs. They are not a complete list of individual experiments.

instruments.name: Imaging photopolarimeter
instruments.body: Measured brightness and polarisation, scanning Jupiter in strips that could be assembled into images.

instruments.name: Magnetic-field measurements
instruments.body: A helium vector magnetometer sampled the interplanetary field and Jupiter’s magnetic environment.

instruments.name: Particles and plasma
instruments.body: Several detectors studied solar-wind plasma, cosmic rays and particles trapped around Jupiter.

instruments.name: Infrared and ultraviolet
instruments.body: A radiometer and photometer investigated radiation beyond visible light, including atmospheric properties.

instrumentDetails: The spacecraft’s rotation swept a small telescope across the scene. Red- and blue-light scans were processed on Earth; this was not an ordinary frame camera.
Magnetic-field measurements helped locate boundaries where the solar wind interacted with Jupiter’s magnetosphere.
The payload included a plasma analyser, charged-particle and cosmic-ray instruments, a Geiger tube telescope and radiation detectors. They sampled different energies and populations.
Infrared measurements added thermal information, while ultraviolet observations probed emission and absorption. Different wavelengths answered different questions.

communication.title: A faint signal is not a data stream
communication.body: NASA’s Deep Space Network detected the final signal on 23 January 2003 at a reported Earth distance of about 12.23 billion kilometres. It was too weak to return telemetry; the last telemetry was received in April 2002.
communication.note: The calculator starts with that historical example distance. It does not show Pioneer 10’s current position or an active radio link.

quiz.title: Could you follow the first pathfinder?
quiz.intro: Three questions about the route, the spacecraft and its last message.
quiz.incorrect: Here is what the mission tells us.

questions.question: Which planet did Pioneer 10 fly past?
questions.explanation: Pioneer 10 made the first Jupiter flyby. Passing Neptune’s orbital distance later did not mean it visited Neptune.

questions.question: What supplied electricity far from the Sun?
questions.explanation: RTGs converted heat from radioactive decay into electricity. They were not solar panels or a fission reactor.

questions.question: Did the final detected signal in 2003 contain usable telemetry?
options: Yes, a complete instrument data set
No, it was a very faint radio signal
questions.explanation: The final carrier signal was detected in January 2003; the last telemetry had been received in April 2002.

faq.question: Did Pioneer 10 confirm that it crossed the heliopause?
faq.answer: No confirmed crossing was measured by the spacecraft. An outward escape trajectory, passing beyond planetary orbits and crossing the heliopause are different events.

faq.question: How did it work without large solar panels?
faq.answer: Radioisotope thermoelectric generators used heat from radioactive decay to produce electricity. Declining available power eventually limited communication.

faq.question: Is the Pioneer plaque a radio transmitter?
faq.answer: No. It is a passive engraved metal message with human figures, a spacecraft outline and astronomical reference diagrams. It could only be read if something physically encountered the spacecraft.

flyby.title: A turn can change your speed
flyby.intro: Rotate an idealised outgoing velocity vector. Compare a moving planet with a hypothetical stationary one to see why the reference frame matters.
flyby.diagram: Incoming and outgoing velocity-vector diagrams, adding planet motion to the spacecraft velocity relative to the planet
flyby.vectorRule: Sun-relative velocity = planet velocity + planet-relative velocity
flyby.planetVector: Planet motion relative to the Sun
flyby.movingExplanation: The far-field speed relative to the planet stays at 10 km/s. Adding a moving planet’s velocity can change the speed relative to the Sun. Energy is exchanged with the planet; it is not created.
flyby.stationaryExplanation: With planet motion set to zero, the incoming and outgoing speeds are both 10 km/s in this model. The direction changes, but there is no lasting speed gain.
flyby.note: Synthetic velocity-vector experiment: planet speed 13 km/s or 0, spacecraft far-field planet-relative speed 10 km/s. Vectors share a linear scale. No encounter orbit, altitude or travel time is calculated. These are not measured Pioneer speeds. The temporary acceleration near closest approach is not shown.
flyby.context: For Pioneer 10, the Jupiter encounter helped establish an outward escape trajectory. This simplified experiment explains the principle, not its actual encounter geometry.

pioneer11.name: Pioneer 11
pioneer11.eyebrow: NASA · Ames Research Center · Jupiter & Saturn · 1973–1995
pioneer11.intro: Pioneer 11 followed the trail to Jupiter, then bent its route toward a second giant. Its first close exploration of Saturn revealed a ring, measured the magnetic environment and helped prepare the way for Voyager.
pioneer11.heroAlt: Pioneer spacecraft with dish antenna and long instrument booms
pioneer11.modelNote: The 3D view uses NASA’s Pioneer 10 model to illustrate the shared basic design. Pioneer 11’s payload and some details differed.

status.title: Mission ended · 1995
status.body: Routine operations ended on 30 September 1995. A final brief engineering-data reception followed on 24 November. The spacecraft is no longer in contact; this page presents its historical mission.

stats.label: Mission lifetime
stats.note: Last engineering data received in November 1995

exploration.eyebrow: A different route for the sister spacecraft
exploration.title: From Jupiter to the ringed planet
exploration.intro: Choose a chapter to see how a mission initially backing up Pioneer 10 became the first to fly past Saturn.
exploration.description: Schematic Pioneer 11 route from Earth to Jupiter, curving toward Saturn before continuing outward
exploration.note: Illustrative route: planet positions, distances and bends are not to scale. The markers select historical topics, not current spacecraft coordinates.

stops.name: The sister spacecraft
stops.body: Pioneer 11 began as a follow-up to Pioneer 10. The success of the first Jupiter encounter allowed planners to extend the second mission toward Saturn.
stops.factLabel: Launch of the second outer-planet Pioneer
stops.question: The two spacecraft shared a basic design, but their instrument complements and flight paths were not identical.

stops.name: A turn at Jupiter
stops.body: The December 1974 encounter returned views of Jupiter’s polar regions. Jupiter’s gravity redirected the trajectory for the long crossing to Saturn.
stops.factLabel: From the Jupiter encounter to Saturn
stops.question: A gravity assist changes the spacecraft’s velocity relative to the Sun by exchanging orbital energy with a moving planet.

stops.name: First at Saturn
stops.body: On 1 September 1979, Pioneer 11 flew close to Saturn and sampled its environment. It detected the narrow F ring and investigated the planet’s magnetic field.
stops.factLabel: Closest approach above Saturn’s cloud tops
stops.question: Pioneer 11 was a flyby spacecraft. Cassini would become Saturn’s first orbiter many years later.

stops.name: The outward journey
stops.body: After Saturn, the spacecraft continued outward, crossing Neptune’s orbital distance in 1990. Declining power and antenna-pointing limitations eventually ended communication.
stops.question: The spacecraft continues on its trajectory even though it no longer returns observations to Earth.

timeline.title: A second Pioneer departs
timeline.body: The Atlas-Centaur launches from Cape Canaveral late on 5 April local time, already 6 April in UTC.

timeline.title: Jupiter changes the route
timeline.body: A close flyby reveals the polar regions and redirects Pioneer 11 toward Saturn.

timeline.title: The first Saturn encounter
timeline.body: The probe studies the rings, atmosphere and magnetic environment during a passage above the cloud tops.

timeline.title: A final brief data reception
timeline.body: After routine operations end on 30 September, a few final minutes of engineering data reach Earth in November.

pioneer11.scienceIntro: Pioneer 11 linked an ambitious route with the first direct measurements at the ringed planet.

science.title: A narrow ring beyond the A ring
science.body: Pioneer 11 detected Saturn’s F ring, adding a new feature to a system that looked much simpler from Earth.

science.title: A magnetic environment around Saturn
science.body: Field and particle measurements established the magnetic environment and boundaries shaped by the solar wind. The encounter added much more than photographs.

science.title: A new view of Jupiter
science.body: The route near Jupiter provided views of the polar regions and cloud structures, extending the picture returned by Pioneer 10 a year earlier.

pioneer11.instrumentIntro: These four groups summarise selected science capabilities. They group several detectors rather than counting every experiment.

instruments.name: Imaging photopolarimeter
instruments.body: Recorded brightness and polarisation, producing scanned views of Jupiter, Saturn and their surroundings.

instruments.name: Magnetometers
instruments.body: Helium-vector and fluxgate measurements investigated magnetic fields and their boundaries.

instruments.name: Plasma and energetic particles
instruments.body: Detectors sampled solar-wind plasma and charged particles in the giant planets’ environments.

instruments.name: Infrared and ultraviolet
instruments.body: Measurements beyond visible light helped investigate atmospheric and thermal properties.

instrumentDetails: Like its sister spacecraft, Pioneer 11 scanned scenes as it rotated. Images were assembled from measurements on Earth, rather than exposed as modern digital camera frames.
Pioneer 11 carried an additional fluxgate magnetometer as well as a helium vector magnetometer. These measurements helped investigate Saturn’s magnetic environment.
Plasma, cosmic-ray, charged-particle and radiation instruments measured populations with different energies. They revealed conditions that pictures alone could not show.
Infrared observations measured thermal radiation; ultraviolet observations supplied complementary information. Radio tracking and occultations also contributed to the mission’s science.

communication.eyebrow: A spacecraft that could no longer point home
communication.title: The final year of radio contact
communication.body: Routine operations ended on 30 September 1995. NASA received a final brief interval of engineering data on 24 November, but declining power and antenna geometry prevented sustained contact.
communication.note: The calculator starts with an illustrative 6.4-billion-kilometre Earth distance, characteristic of the mission’s final era. It is not a current measurement or an active connection.

quiz.title: Ready for the ringed planet?
quiz.intro: Three questions about the route and what a flyby can reveal.
quiz.incorrect: Here is what the mission tells us.

questions.question: Which planet did Pioneer 11 visit after Jupiter?
questions.explanation: Jupiter’s gravity redirected Pioneer 11 toward the first spacecraft flyby of Saturn in September 1979.

questions.question: Did Pioneer 11 enter orbit around Saturn?
questions.explanation: Pioneer 11 passed Saturn and continued outward. It was not a Saturn orbiter.

questions.question: What is a gravity assist exchanging with the planet?
questions.explanation: A moving planet can exchange orbital energy and momentum with a spacecraft. The effect on the much more massive planet is tiny.

faq.question: Was Pioneer 11 the first spacecraft at Saturn?
faq.answer: Yes. Its September 1979 flyby preceded Voyager 1, Voyager 2 and Cassini. Cassini later became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn.

faq.question: Why are both September and November 1995 mentioned?
faq.answer: Routine operations ended on 30 September. A final brief reception of engineering data took place on 24 November. These describe different milestones in the end of the mission.

faq.question: Did passing Neptune’s orbit mean it visited Neptune?
faq.answer: No. Pioneer 11 crossed Neptune’s orbital distance in February 1990, without a close encounter with that planet. A heliopause crossing was not confirmed by measurements from Pioneer 11.

flyby.vectorRule: Sun-relative velocity = planet velocity + planet-relative velocity
flyby.planetVector: Planet motion relative to the Sun
